name: Low Lunar Polar Orbit (LLO · 100 km)
goodAt: Flies directly over both North and South lunar poles on every 118-minute orbit with sharp surface resolution (modeled on NASA LRO).
badAt: Lunar gravity anomalies ('mascons') perturb 100 km polar orbits over time, requiring station-keeping propellant.
hintText: A 90° polar orbit passes over Shackleton and Peary craters every two hours while the Moon slowly rotates underneath.
sourceLabel: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) 50–100 km Polar Mapping Orbit

name: Elliptical Polar Frozen Orbit (50 × 200 km)
goodAt: Skims just 50 km above the South Pole craters while remaining gravitationally stable for years without burning fuel.
badAt: Higher altitude over the North Pole slightly reduces northern resolution compared to a circular 50 km orbit.
hintText: NASA uses 'frozen' lunar orbits so spacecraft can map the South Pole for years without crashing into lunar mountains.
sourceLabel: NASA GSFC — LRO Quasi-Frozen South Pole Orbit Design

name: Low Lunar Equatorial Orbit (100 km · 15°)
goodAt: Repeatedly observes low-latitude Apollo landing sites and equatorial maria.
badAt: Never reaches latitudes above 15° — completely misses the Permanently Shadowed Regions at the lunar poles!
hintText: Warning: An equatorial orbit cannot see inside polar craters. For Ice Hunter, choose a high-inclination polar orbit.
sourceLabel: NASA Planetary Data System — Lunar Orbit Mechanics
